fields.Front: What does Spring's @Async annotation do to a method call?
fields.Back: Causes the method to execute on a separate thread from a configured TaskExecutor instead of the caller's thread, so the caller doesn't block waiting for it. Requires @EnableAsync on a configuration class.

fields.Front: How do you code an asynchronous Spring service method that returns a result?
fields.Back:
@Service
public class ValidationService {
    @Async
    public CompletableFuture<Boolean> validateAsync(EForm form) {
        boolean valid = runValidation(form);
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(valid);
    }
}

fields.Front: Why does an @Async method typically return CompletableFuture<T> (or void) rather than T directly?
fields.Back: Because the method runs on another thread and the caller returns immediately; CompletableFuture gives the caller a handle to later retrieve the result or compose further async work, while void is used for fire-and-forget calls.

fields.Front: What happens if you call an @Async method from another method in the same class (self-invocation)?
fields.Back: The @Async annotation is ignored — Spring's proxy-based AOP only intercepts calls made through the external bean reference, so an internal call bypasses the proxy and executes synchronously on the caller's thread.

fields.Front: What is a thread pool (Executor), and why use one instead of spawning a new thread per task?
fields.Back: A managed pool of reusable worker threads that pull tasks from a queue; reusing threads avoids the overhead of constantly creating/destroying OS threads and lets you bound concurrency to avoid exhausting system resources.

fields.Front: How do you configure a custom thread pool for @Async tasks in Spring?
fields.Back:
@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class AsyncConfig {
    @Bean(name = "taskExecutor")
    public Executor taskExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        executor.setCorePoolSize(8);
        executor.setMaxPoolSize(16);
        executor.setQueueCapacity(100);
        return executor;
    }
}

fields.Front: What does "non-blocking I/O" mean, and why did the Gov of Ontario eForm validation microservice use it with @Async?
fields.Back: The thread that issues an I/O operation (network/DB call) isn't left idle waiting for it — it's freed to do other work while the I/O completes in the background. Combined with Spring @Async, this kept worker threads from blocking on slow validation calls in a ~10GB/day pipeline, cutting latency by 40%.

fields.Front: What is CompletableFuture used for in Java concurrency?
fields.Back: A Future implementation that lets you compose, chain, and combine asynchronous computations (thenApply, thenCompose, allOf, thenCombine, etc.) without manually blocking a thread to wait for a result.

fields.Front: How do you run two independent tasks concurrently and combine their results with CompletableFuture?
fields.Back:
CompletableFuture<Integer> f1 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> slowLookup());
CompletableFuture<Integer> f2 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> anotherLookup());
CompletableFuture<Integer> combined = f1.thenCombine(f2, Integer::sum);
combined.thenAccept(System.out::println);
A bug where a program's correctness depends on the relative timing/interleaving of multiple threads accessing shared mutable state, producing incorrect results under certain thread orderings.

fields.Front: Name two standard ways to prevent a race condition on shared mutable state in Java.
fields.Back: Synchronize access (the synchronized keyword or explicit locks) so only one thread mutates the state at a time, or use atomic/concurrent-safe types (e.g. AtomicInteger, ConcurrentHashMap) that are designed for lock-free thread-safe updates.

fields.Front: What is the circuit breaker pattern used for in a microservice architecture?
fields.Back: It stops a service from repeatedly calling a downstream dependency that is failing or slow, by "tripping" after a failure threshold and short-circuiting further calls (failing fast) instead of piling up latency and exhausting resources.

fields.Front: How do you apply a Resilience4j circuit breaker with a fallback to a method in Spring Boot?
fields.Back:
@CircuitBreaker(name = "eformValidation", fallbackMethod = "fallback")
public ValidationResult callValidationService(EForm form) {
    return restTemplate.postForObject(url, form, ValidationResult.class);
}

public ValidationResult fallback(EForm form, Throwable t) {
    return ValidationResult.unavailable();
}

fields.Front: What is the difference between Resilience4j's retry and bulkhead patterns?
fields.Back: Retry automatically re-attempts a failed call a configured number of times (often with backoff), aiming to survive transient failures. Bulkhead limits the number of concurrent calls to a dependency (via a semaphore or fixed thread pool), isolating it so its slowness/failures can't exhaust resources the rest of the app needs.

fields.Front: What does a rate limiter do in Resilience4j, and why pair one with a downstream call?
fields.Back: It caps how many calls are allowed to a resource within a time window, rejecting or delaying calls beyond that limit — protecting both the caller and the downstream service from being overwhelmed by traffic spikes.

fields.Front: What is Caffeine, and what problem does it solve?
fields.Back: A high-performance, in-memory Java caching library; it avoids recomputing or refetching expensive/repeated results (e.g. DB lookups) by storing them in memory with configurable size limits and eviction policies.

fields.Front: How do you cache a Spring service method's result with @Cacheable (Caffeine-backed)?
fields.Back:
@Service
public class LookupService {
    @Cacheable(value = "eformTypes", key = "#formId")
    public EFormType getFormType(Long formId) {
        return expensiveLookup(formId);
    }
}
Backed by a CaffeineCacheManager bean configured with cache names, TTL, and max size.

fields.Front: Name two eviction policies Caffeine supports for bounding cache size or lifetime.
fields.Back: Size-based eviction (maximumSize, evicting least-recently-used entries once a cap is reached) and time-based eviction (expireAfterWrite / expireAfterAccess, evicting entries after a fixed duration).

fields.Front: What's a common gotcha with @Cacheable and self-invocation, similar to @Async?
fields.Back: Calling a @Cacheable method from another method in the same class bypasses Spring's proxy (just like with @Async), so the caching logic never runs and the method executes uncached every time.

fields.Text: A Resilience4j circuit breaker has three core states: {{c1::CLOSED}} (calls pass through normally while failures are counted), {{c2::OPEN}} (calls are short-circuited immediately without reaching the downstream service), and {{c3::HALF_OPEN}} (a limited number of trial calls are let through to test if the dependency has recovered).
fields.Extra: OPEN transitions to HALF_OPEN after a configured wait duration; HALF_OPEN moves to CLOSED on success or back to OPEN on failure.
